newsitem.title: HONG KONG: China says will not allow mainland influx into HK.
newsitem.headline: China says will not allow mainland influx into HK.

text.p: Chinese officials on Friday sought to assure Hong Kong there will be no flood of mainlanders into the territory after Beijing resumes control this year and that the Chinese army garrison stationed here will behave.
They also tried to calm fears that the economy in the freewheeling capitalist enclave will suffer and stressed the importance of allowing Hong Kong businessmen to travel.
Hong Kong reverts to communist-ruled China at midnight on June 30 after more than 150 years of British rule.

Under China's "one country, two systems" policy, Hong Kong has been promised a high degree of autonomy for 50 years after the handover, but pro-democracy activists across the world have expressed fears about human rights and press freedom.
Wang Fengchao, deputy chief of Beijing's Hong Kong and Macau Affairs Office, dismissed fears that China would open the floodgates to Chinese seeking to cash in on Hong Kong's economic success.
He said there were strict procedures for approving entry into Hong Kong and that children of illegal immigrants would not be allowed in.
"These provisions...will have a deterrent effect," he said.
Wang was speaking at a seminar marking the seventh anniversary of the proclamation of the Basic Law, the mini-constitution for the future Hong Kong Special Administrative Region of China.
Major-General Xiong Zi Ren, political commissar of the People's Liberation Army garrison to be stationed in Hong Kong after the handover, said his soldiers would be on their best behaviour.
"The garrison shall act as ordinary members of Hong Kong society and abide by Hong Kong laws as well as by military discipline," Xiong said.
Their priorities would include "to treasure" public and private property in Hong Kong and to "observe social morality and civic politeness".
"The PLA garrison in Hong Kong will certainly strive to live up to the expectations of our motherland and our people, as well as to the satisfaction of our Hong Kong compatriots," he said.

The handover has triggered fears about the territory's political future, especially after China's decision to dismantle the elected Legislative Council and replace it with a Beijing-anointed provisional body.
The U.S. State Department this week said developments in Hong Kong were sending "mixed signals".
Wang, of the Hong Kong and Macau Affairs Office, sought to assure Hong Kong people on nationality issues and said foreign passports would not bar Chinese citizens in Hong Kong from travelling abroad.
"We hold that one of the important conditions to maintain prosperity and stability in Hong Kong is to ensure the convenience for Hong Kong people to go abroad for business," he said.
Hong Kong's post-handover leader, Tung Chee-hwa, pinned his hopes on the Basic Law for ensuring the territory's way of life remained unchanged.
"Under the protection of the Basic Law, I have full confidence in one country, two systems and Hong Kong people ruling Hong Kong," he said.

Tung's office has started drafting laws related to the right of abode for non-Chinese foreign passport holders, which he could submit to the provisional legislature by July 1, the Chinese-language Ming Pao newspaper said on Friday.
